skills.name: Great circles and the International Date Line

note.text: A great circle is formed when a plane through Earth's centre cuts its surface, dividing the sphere into equal hemispheres. The Equator is a great circle; a meridian paired with its opposite also forms one. Other parallels are small circles. On a sphere, the shorter great-circle arc gives a shortest surface route between suitable points. The International Date Line is a civil-date boundary broadly near the opposite meridian to Greenwich, with deviations. Crossing it westward adds a day; eastward subtracts a day.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: A great circle is formed when a plane through Earth's centre cuts its surface, dividing the sphere into equal hemispheres. The Equator is a great circle; a meridian paired with its opposite also forms one. Other parallels are small circles. On a sphere, the shorter great-circle arc gives a shortest surface route between suitable points. The International Date Line is a civil-date boundary broadly near the opposite meridian to Greenwich, with deviations. Crossing it westward adds a day; eastward subtracts a day.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: A route drawn straight on a flat world map is not necessarily the shortest route on a globe. A traveller crossing the Date Line must adjust the calendar as well as the clock. A time difference near midnight can also change a date without crossing the line, so keep the two reasons for date changes distinct.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Ask whether the cutting plane passes through the centre. For date exercises, identify travel direction and state the adopted line convention. Actual civil boundaries and standard-time decisions are irregular; do not treat the diagram as an exact map of present national rules.
